# Laṭukikopama Sutta (MN 66 (PTS MN i 447))

**ID:** MN 66 (PTS MN i 447)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Laṭukikopama Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Simile of the Quail
**PTS:** MN i 447
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn66
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Laṭukikopama Sutta* ("The Simile of the Quail") is the 66th discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* (PTS MN i 447) [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The sutta is set in the country of the Aṅguttarāpas at a town named Āpaṇa [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Its opening context concerns monastic regulations restricting meal times, specifically the rule to abandon eating at night, framed around gratitude toward the Buddha for eliminating conditions that cause complexity and stress [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017a]. Using various similes—including that of the quail—the Buddha illustrates how attachment even to minor or seemingly insignificant things can be dangerous and binding, showing that people often mistakenly gauge the strength of what they cling to by the strength of their attachment [SuttaCentral; Stanley et al. 2018].

A major doctrinal theme of the discourse is the classification of happiness (*sukha*). The Buddha contrasts sensual happiness derived from the five strands of sensuality (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), characterizing it as "dung-happiness" (*mīḷhasukha*) or common, non-noble happiness (*puthujjanasukha*) that should not be pursued, with the bliss of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukha*) and seclusion found in the *jhāna*s, which is suitable to be cultivated, developed, and not feared [Underwood 1973; Saitanaporn 2009; Dhammissara 2017; Brahm]. Progress through the nine successive meditative abidings is described as recognizing each stage as "not enough" and surmounting (*samatikkama*) it [Polak 2011].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include full versions in the Chinese Āgamas (*Madhyama-āgama* MĀ 192 and *Ekottarika-āgama* EĀ 49.7), partial parallels in MN 65 (*Bhaddāli Sutta*), MĀ 194, Sanskrit fragment SHT sutta15, and Vinaya parallels in the Chinese Mahīśāsaka and Dharmaguptaka traditions; it is also mentioned in the Mahāsaṅghika Vinaya and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 16.3) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017a]. Machine analysis by DharmaNexus strongly aligns the sutta with the *Madhyama-āgama* (ZH_T01_0026_050) and demonstrates substantial Pali-internal text reuse with texts treating meditative abidings and monastic restraint, including the *Navakanipāta* (AN 9), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82), and *Bahuvedanīya Sutta* (MN 59) [DharmaNexus].
